title: A JWT signing secret is hardcoded as a string literal in source code instead of being loaded from an environment variable or secret manager
evidence: A JWT signing secret is hardcoded as a string literal in source code instead of being loaded from an environment variable or secret manager. Anyone with read access to the source (or its version control history) can forge valid tokens. Matched code: JWT_SECRET = "secret123"
recommendation: Load the signing secret from an environment variable or a secrets manager at runtime, and rotate it if it has ever been committed to version control.

title: A JWT algorithms allowlist includes "none", which permits an attacker to forge a token with an empty signature that will still be accepted as valid
evidence: A JWT algorithms allowlist includes "none", which permits an attacker to forge a token with an empty signature that will still be accepted as valid. Matched code: JWT_ALGORITHMS = ["HS256", "none"]
recommendation: Pin the accepted algorithm list to only the algorithm(s) the application actually signs with (e.g. ["HS256"]), and never include "none" â€” the JWT spec's unsigned-token option.

title: pickle.loads() is called on data that may come from an untrusted source
evidence: pickle.loads() is called on data that may come from an untrusted source. Python's pickle format can execute arbitrary code during deserialization (via __reduce__), so calling pickle.loads() on attacker-controlled input allows remote code execution. Matched code: obj = pickle.loads(raw_bytes)  # VULNERABLE
recommendation: Never deserialize untrusted data with pickle. Use a safe, data-only format such as JSON instead, or if a binary format is required, use one without arbitrary code execution on load (e.g. protobuf with a fixed schema).
